chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Abdullah ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I said to him (about the verse): 'They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God' [9:31].

So he said: By God, they did not call them to worship themselves, and even if they had called them, they would not have responded. But they permitted for them what was forbidden, and forbade upon them what was permissible, and thus they worshipped them from an aspect they were not aware of.

key_terms.أَحَلُّوا وَحَرَّمُوا: They permitted and they forbade; the act of legislating halal/haram in place of God
key_terms.أَحْبَار: Rabbis, Jewish scholars; those with religious knowledge and authority
key_terms.أَرْبَاب: Lords, masters; those whose authority is obeyed as if divine
key_terms.رُهْبَان: Monks, Christian ascetics; those devoted to religious practice
key_terms.عِبَادَة: Worship, servitude; the act of submitting to another's authority

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about taking scholars as lords besides God (Quran 9:31)?
ai.summary: Abu Basir asks Imam al-Sadiq (AS) about Quran 9:31, which describes how the People of the Book took their rabbis and monks as lords besides God. The Imam clarifies that this worship was not explicit idol-worship — the priests never literally demanded to be worshipped. Rather, by exercising the authority to make halal what is haram and haram what is halal, they usurped God's exclusive legislative prerogative, and their followers' obedience constituted an indirect form of worship. This constitutes a foundational Shia argument against blind taqlid of any religious authority who deviates from divine law.
word_analysis: they would have responded to them
